items.title: The Act, the Appointed Day & the Capital Question
items.body:
### How the Reorganisation Act set up two states

**In one line**
The AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 is the law that split united Andhra Pradesh — it fixed the date, named the two states, decided who kept Hyderabad, and divided the seats between them.

**Why it is asked**
The appointed day, Section 5 (Hyderabad for ten years), the Sivaramakrishnan capital committee and the seat split are among the most-asked single facts from this topic.

**The story**
Parliament passed the **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014** and the President gave assent on **1 March 2014**. But a law can name a later start date, and here the **'appointed day' — the day the split actually happened — was 2 June 2014**. On that day a new state of **Telangana** was formed (Section 3) from 10 districts, while the leftover state kept the name **Andhra Pradesh** (Section 4), holding the Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema regions.

To manage the handover, the Act gave both states a **common Governor** for a period the President would decide (Section 7), with **special responsibility for law and order in Hyderabad** (Section 8).

The thorniest question was the capital. **Section 5** made **Hyderabad the common capital for a period not exceeding 10 years**, after which it becomes Telangana's alone and AP must have its own. To help AP choose, **Section 6** required the Centre to set up an **expert committee** within six months; it was chaired by **K.C. Sivaramakrishnan**, which cautioned against a single mega-capital. AP nonetheless chose **Amaravati**, a greenfield capital built on pooled farmland.

Finally, political power was divided in proportion to population.

**Picture it**

| Body | Undivided AP | Andhra Pradesh | Telangana |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lok Sabha | 42 | 25 | 17 |
| Assembly | 294 | 175 | 119 |

**Terms explained**
- **Appointed day** — the date fixed by the central government on which the new state legally comes into being (here 2 June 2014).
- **Residuary state** — the state left after a new one is carved out (the new Andhra Pradesh).
- **Common capital** — a single city serving both states temporarily; here Hyderabad, for up to 10 years.
- **Common Governor** — one Governor shared by both successor states during the transition.
- **Greenfield capital** — a capital built from scratch on fresh land (Amaravati).

**Don't confuse**
- The **assent date (1 March 2014)** is NOT the appointed day — the split took effect on **2 June 2014**.
- The **Sivaramakrishnan Committee studied capital options**; it did not pick Amaravati — the AP government did.

**Remember it**
'2-6-14' = **2 June 2014** appointed day; Hyderabad's common-capital clock runs **10 years, to June 2024**.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Appointed day | 2 June 2014 — Telangana formed, residuary AP remains |
| Section 5 | Hyderabad common capital for up to 10 years |
| Section 6 | Sivaramakrishnan committee on the new capital |
| Seats | AP 25 LS / 175 Assembly; Telangana 17 / 119 |
keyPoints: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 assented 1 March 2014; appointed day = 2 June 2014 (Telangana formed).
Section 5: Hyderabad is the common capital for a period not exceeding 10 years.
Section 6 expert committee on the new capital was headed by K.C. Sivaramakrishnan.
AP chose Amaravati as its greenfield capital via land pooling.
Seats: AP got 25 Lok Sabha & 175 Assembly; Telangana 17 & 119 (of erstwhile 42 & 294).
items.mnemonic: '2-6-14' = 2 June 2014 appointed day; capital clock runs 10 years to June 2024.

items.title: Division of Assets, Liabilities, Institutions & Employees
items.body:
### Splitting the money, bodies and staff of one state into two

**In one line**
When one state becomes two, everything it owned and owed — cash, companies, buildings, staff and central grants — has to be divided, and the Act lays down the rules for each.

**Why it is asked**
The population-ratio rule, the Ninth vs Tenth Schedule distinction, the Kamalanathan employee committee, and the Section 46 finance-commission provisions are standard match and statement questions.

**The story**
Money and movable things were split mainly by the **population ratio** (about **58:42, AP:Telangana**), while **immovable property went to whichever state it physically sits in** — a building in Hyderabad stays with Telangana, one in Visakhapatnam with AP. To handle the many state-owned bodies, the Act used two lists: the **Ninth Schedule** names the **government companies and corporations** to be divided, and the **Tenth Schedule** names **institutions whose facilities both states keep using** (training institutes, for example).

**People** were the hardest part. Lakhs of employees of the old state had to be allotted to one state or the other, and 'who belongs where' (nativity/local-cadre) disputes flared up. A central advisory committee under **Kamalanathan** framed the guidelines and finalised the allocation.

Finally, **fiscal transition** was handled under **Section 46**: the award of the **Thirteenth Finance Commission** was shared between the two new states, and the President referred the matter to the **Fourteenth Finance Commission** for **fresh, separate awards**. The 14th FC later gave AP a **revenue-deficit grant** to help plug its post-bifurcation gap, and the Centre was to consider a **special development package** focused on **Rayalaseema and the north-coastal regions**.

**Picture it**

| Item | How it was divided |
|---|---|
| Cash, movable assets | Population ratio (~58:42) |
| Immovable property | Goes to the state where it is located |
| Companies/corporations | Ninth Schedule |
| Shared institutions | Tenth Schedule |
| Employees | Kamalanathan Committee guidelines |

**Terms explained**
- **Population ratio** — dividing in proportion to each state's population (~58% AP, ~42% Telangana).
- **Movable vs immovable** — cash and equipment (movable) versus land and buildings (immovable, split by location).
- **Ninth Schedule** — the list of state government companies and corporations to be apportioned.
- **Tenth Schedule** — the list of institutions whose facilities continue to serve both states.
- **Revenue-deficit grant** — a Finance Commission grant to a state whose revenue falls short of its revenue spending.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ninth Schedule = companies/corporations; Tenth Schedule = shared institutions** — do not swap them.
- The **Finance Commission** handled fiscal transfers; it did NOT divide physical assets (that was by population/location).

**Remember it**
'Cash by heads, buildings by place': movable split ~58:42, immovable by location; 9th = companies, 10th = institutions.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Assets | Movable by population ~58:42; immovable by location |
| Schedules | Ninth = companies; Tenth = shared institutions |
| Employees | Allotted via the Kamalanathan Committee |
| Section 46 | 13th FC award shared; referred to 14th FC for new awards |
keyPoints: Assets split mainly by population ratio (~58:42); immovable assets go to the State where located.
Ninth Schedule = government companies/corporations; Tenth Schedule = institutions with continued facilities.
Employee allocation between AP and Telangana was guided by the Kamalanathan Committee.
Section 46: 13th FC award apportioned; President to refer to 14th FC for separate awards.
Special development package to focus on Rayalaseema and north-coastal regions (s.46).
items.source: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (s.46, s.68-77, Ninth & Tenth Schedules); Kamalanathan Committee

items.title: Water Management & Polavaram (National Project)
items.body:
### How the Act manages shared rivers and the Polavaram dam

**In one line**
Because the Krishna and Godavari flow through both new states, the Act set up two river boards and a tribunal to share the water, and declared the Polavaram dam a national project.

**Why it is asked**
The two boards and their headquarters (Section 85), Polavaram's national-project status (Section 90), and Sections 89/91 are frequent Prelims facts and the core of water-sharing Mains answers.

**The story**
Rivers do not respect new borders, so the Act created two referee bodies under the Union: the **Krishna River Management Board (KRMB)** and the **Godavari River Management Board (GRMB)**, under **Section 85**. Their **headquarters were deliberately split — KRMB in Andhra Pradesh and GRMB in Telangana** — and they work on the principles of the **Eleventh Schedule**, under which earlier Krishna tribunal awards bind both states.

Two more sections tidied up older arrangements: **Section 89** extended the term of the **Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (KWDT)** so it could settle leftover issues, and **Section 91** put both successor states (in place of the old one) on the **Tungabhadra Board**, which oversees releases to the High Level Canal, Low Level Canal and Rajolibanda Diversion Scheme.

The centrepiece is **Section 90**, which declares the **Polavaram Irrigation Project** on the **Godavari** a **national project**. This means the **Union takes control** of regulating and developing it, **Telangana's consent is treated as already given**, and the Centre is to execute the work and obtain all clearances. In practice, execution was handed to AP in 2016 on a **reimbursement** basis, and the **funding scope (whether at 2013-14 or revised costs)** and resettlement remain a live AP-Centre dispute.

**Picture it**

| Board | Headquarters |
|---|---|
| Krishna River Management Board (KRMB) | Andhra Pradesh |
| Godavari River Management Board (GRMB) | Telangana |

**Terms explained**
- **River Management Board** — a central body overseeing the sharing and operation of a shared inter-state river.
- **Eleventh Schedule** — the part of the Act laying down the principles the two boards must follow.
- **Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (KWDT)** — the tribunal that adjudicates how Krishna water is shared.
- **National project** — a project the Centre controls and largely funds in the public interest.
- **Reimbursement basis** — the state spends first and the Centre repays the approved cost later.

**Don't confuse**
- **KRMB sits in AP; GRMB sits in Telangana** — easy to reverse.
- Section 90 says the **Union executes** Polavaram; the later 2016 hand-over to AP is an administrative change, not the Act's text.

**Remember it**
Boards swap sides: **KRMB = AP, GRMB = Telangana**; Polavaram = **Section 90, national project**.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Section 85 | Created KRMB (HQ AP) and GRMB (HQ Telangana) |
| Section 89 / 91 | Extended the Krishna tribunal; both states on Tungabhadra Board |
| Section 90 | Polavaram (Godavari) declared a national project |
| Dispute | Polavaram funding scope and R&R still contested |
keyPoints: Section 85 created KRMB and GRMB; KRMB HQ in AP, GRMB HQ in Telangana.
Section 89 extended the Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal term; Eleventh Schedule sets Board principles.
Section 91: both States replace undivided AP on the Tungabhadra Board.
Section 90 declared the Polavaram Irrigation Project (on the Godavari) a national project.
Under s.90 the Union executes Polavaram and Telangana's consent is deemed given; funding remains disputed.
items.mnemonic: Boards swap sides: KRMB=AP, GRMB=Telangana (Krishna flows more to AP's core).
items.source: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (s.85, s.89, s.90, s.91, Eleventh Schedule)

items.title: Thirteenth Schedule Commitments, SCS Debate & Status (2026)
items.body:
### What AP was promised — and what has actually happened

**In one line**
To make up for losing Hyderabad, the Act promised AP a long list of institutions and infrastructure in the Thirteenth Schedule, plus a disputed demand for Special Category Status that was never granted.

**Why it is asked**
The Thirteenth-Schedule institutions, the Dugarajupatnam/Kadapa infrastructure promises, and the SCS-versus-Special-Package debate are repeatedly tested, especially 'what is or is not in the Act'.

**The story**
The **Thirteenth Schedule (Section 93)** is the Act's compensation list. For **education and health** it promised AP one each of an **IIT, NIT, IIM, IISER, Central University, Petroleum University, Agricultural University and IIIT**, plus an **AIIMS-type super-specialty hospital**, a **Tribal University** and the **National Institute of Disaster Management**. For **infrastructure** it promised a new **major port at Dugarajupatnam**, an **integrated steel plant in YSR (Kadapa) district**, the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC)** — India's first coastal economic corridor — a **new railway zone**, and upgrades to the **Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada and Tirupati airports**.

The loudest controversy, though, is over something **not in the Act at all: Special Category Status (SCS)**. SCS was only a **spoken assurance by the Prime Minister on the floor of the Rajya Sabha in February 2014**. After the **Fourteenth Finance Commission** effectively ended SCS for states outside the North-East and hills, the Centre in **2016 offered a Special Package** (funding via externally-aided projects) instead. AP considers this inadequate, so the demand stays politically alive.

**Picture it (status as of 2026)**

| Commitment | Status |
|---|---|
| Central institutions (IIT Tirupati, IIM Vizag, IISER Tirupati, Central University) | Largely established |
| New railway zone (South Coast Railway, HQ Visakhapatnam) | Sanctioned 2019; operational since 1 June 2026 |
| Polavaram national project | Under execution; funding disputed |
| Dugarajupatnam port | Effectively dropped/unrealised |
| Kadapa steel plant | Scaled/partial, not completed as an integrated plant |
| Special Category Status | Not granted (Special Package offered) |

**Terms explained**
- **Thirteenth Schedule** — the Act's list of institutions and infrastructure promised to the successor states.
- **Special Category Status (SCS)** — a status giving a state higher central grants (90% grant share historically); AP never received it.
- **Special Package (2016)** — the Centre's SCS substitute, funding AP projects through externally-aided-project reimbursement.
- **Externally-aided project (EAP)** — a project funded with loans from bodies like the World Bank, where the Centre bears repayment.
- **South Coast Railway (SCoR)** — India's 18th railway zone, HQ Visakhapatnam, operational from 1 June 2026.

**Don't confuse**
- **SCS was NOT in the Act** — only a Rajya Sabha assurance; the Act promised a *special development package*, not SCS.
- The Dugarajupatnam **port** and Kadapa **steel plant** were promised to **AP**; the Rail Coach Factory and the 4000 MW NTPC plant were for **Telangana**.

**Remember it**
'Promised vs delivered': institutions and the railway zone largely done; port, steel plant and SCS still pending.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Thirteenth Schedule | AP's promised institutions + infrastructure |
| Done | IIT/IIM/IISER/Central Univ; South Coast Railway (live 1 Jun 2026) |
| Pending | Dugarajupatnam port, Kadapa steel plant, Polavaram funding |
| SCS | Never in the Act; not granted; Special Package (2016) instead |
keyPoints: Thirteenth Schedule promised AP an IIT, NIT, IIM, IISER, Central University, AIIMS-type institution and Tribal University.
AP infrastructure promises: Dugarajupatnam port, Kadapa (YSR) steel plant, VCIC corridor, a new railway zone, airport upgrades.
Special Category Status was a Rajya Sabha assurance (Feb 2014), not part of the Act.
14th FC ended SCS for most states; Centre offered a Special Package (2016) with EAP funding instead.
South Coast Railway zone (HQ Visakhapatnam) was sanctioned in 2019 and became operational on 1 June 2026; Dugarajupatnam port and Kadapa steel plant remain unrealised.
items.source: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Thirteenth Schedule, s.93-94); Special Package 2016; Ministry of Railways (South Coast Railway zone, sanctioned 2019, operational 1 Jun 2026)

items.title: For Mains — AP Reorganisation Act: Economic Issues
items.body:
### For Mains — bifurcation, commitments and federal finance

Mains Paper-4 (clauses **M4-3** resource mobilisation in AP — bifurcation, external assistance, water disputes; **M4-5** AP budgeting constraints) and Paper-2 (**M2-10** bifurcation impacts, capital, employees, river water) draw directly on this subtopic. Frame answers on one thread: **the Act created both a settlement mechanism and a bundle of promises, and AP's economy is still shaped by how fully those promises are honoured.**

**Dimensions the examiner expects**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Settlement machinery | Appointed day, asset/liability split (population + location), employees (Kamalanathan) |
| Water architecture | KRMB/GRMB (s.85), KWDT (s.89), Tungabhadra (s.91), Polavaram national project (s.90) |
| Promises (Sch. XIII) | Institutions, Dugarajupatnam port, Kadapa steel, VCIC, railway zone, airports |
| Fiscal transition | s.46 (13th→14th FC), revenue-deficit grant, special development package |
| SCS debate | Rajya Sabha assurance vs 14th-FC-era Special Package (2016); federalism tension |
| Way forward | Cooperative federalism, clear Polavaram costing, delivering pending commitments |

**Data points, provisions and status to quote**
- Appointed day 2 June 2014; Hyderabad common capital up to 10 years (s.5); AP 25 LS / 175 Assembly seats.
- Polavaram: national project (s.90), under execution, targeted before the 2027 Godavari Pushkarams; Budget 2026-27 allots ₹6,105 cr.
- Amaravati: WB + ADB ~USD 1,600 mn (Phase-1), Budget 2026-27 ₹6,000 cr, implemented by APCRDA.
- South Coast Railway (18th zone, HQ Visakhapatnam) sanctioned 2019, operational 1 June 2026 — a statutory commitment delivered.
- 16th Finance Commission (2026-31): AP's divisible-pool share 4.22% — ordinary, not special-category, treatment.

**Use in answers**
- **Example:** contrast a delivered commitment (South Coast Railway, operational 2026) with an unrealised one (Dugarajupatnam port) to show uneven implementation.
- **Quote:** stress that SCS was an assurance 'on the floor of the House', not a statutory right — the heart of the AP-Centre federalism debate.
- **Diagram idea:** a two-column 'promised versus delivered (2026)' table, or a water-architecture flow (Apex Council → KRMB/GRMB → KWDT) to show institutional design.
keyPoints: Thread: the Act is both a settlement mechanism and a bundle of promises still shaping AP's economy.
Cover settlement (assets/employees), water architecture (s.85/89/90/91) and Thirteenth-Schedule promises.
Quote s.46 fiscal transition, revenue-deficit grant, and the 16th FC 4.22% share as federal-finance evidence.
Use the SCS-versus-Special-Package debate to discuss cooperative federalism.
Contrast delivered (South Coast Railway 2026) with pending (Dugarajupatnam port, Kadapa steel) commitments.
items.source: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (s.5, s.46, s.85-91, Thirteenth Schedule); PRS — AP Budget 2026-27; 16th Finance Commission; Ministry of Railways (verified Sep 2026)
